## The Unfinished Map

The morning arrives without knocking. It seeps under the door like a rumor and finds the floorboards, the rim of the kettle, the pale blue spine of an unread book. Outside, the city is clearing its throat. A bus sighs at the corner. Someone below is watering herbs on a balcony because joy, apparently, can be grown in a railroad planter if you are stubborn and have decent drainage.

I used to think writing was a lighthouse: dramatic, vertical, aimed at storms. Mostly it is a broom. You sweep the same kitchen every day. crumbs of thought, dust of worry, a little glitter from some stranger’s birthday. The trick is not to hate the dust. The trick is to notice that the broom is also a kind of pen, and the floor is a page no one will frame.

There is a map I carry everywhere and drew badly. It shows continents that don’t exist: the Country of Almost, the Province of Later, the Republic of I Once Said I Would. It has rivers labeled now or never and mountains called Overthinking. At the edge, in ink already fading, I wrote Here be Tenderness, because cartographers of the inner life always run out of coastline eventually.

Today the radio said something about distant galaxies. Yesterday I learned that a neighbor retired after thirty years and now feeds pigeons with ceremonial patience. Larger universes do not cancel smaller ones; they lean on them for support. The big bang may still be echoing, but so is the clink of a spoon against a mug, and mine was louder this instant.

By noon, emails had their usual republican enthusiasm for shouting. Meetings multiplied like aphids in warm weather. Somewhere in the middle of a sentence about deliverables, I remembered a boy once told me the moon looked “like a fingerprint on the sky.” No one grades that kind of sentence. No committee approves it. It simply occurs, precise and useless and perfect, and then the real world asks for a status update.

The strange comfort of being human is that we contain both tabs. We can calculate and marvel in the same breath. We can itemize groceries and yet be undone by the fact that in 2064 none of us will have seen this cloud exactly like this, especially if it is shaped, however briefly, like a trout judging horizons. We are magnificent filing cabinets with hearts sneaking out after closing time.

A friend called to say she had planted tomatoes too early, against advice, because hope had ignored the forecast. I admired the tomatoes and the disobedience. Spring is often just instinct with dirt under its nails. We are told to wait until conditions are right, while the whole scandal of being alive is that conditions are never fully right. Seeds do not attend webinars on risk management. They lean toward whatever light is available and do the ancient math of becoming.

In the afternoon I walked nowhere in particular, which is sometimes the most serious destination. The pharmacy sold postcards of sunsets from places I’ve never been. The bakery window offered bread with darkened shoulders and the confidence of things made by someone who knew flour intimately. A man argued gently with a parking meter, lost with dignity, and fed it coins anyway, because civilization depends on losing beautifully.

What are words for? To record, to conjure, to stall, to accuse, to comfort, to put a hand on the shoulder of the exact stranger who will never know. Words are ferry ropes between separate weather systems. Sometimes they fail. Often they hold. Sometimes a single sentence says, “I have been there too,” and a person who was drowning in sound remembers how to breathe.

If this piece must confess anything, it is that attention is a moral act wearing ordinary shoes. To attend is to refuse, briefly, the flattening pressure that everything is interchangeable. Not this cup, not this light, not this tired and glorious animal of a Tuesday, not the way dust becomes visible only when the sun agrees to reveal it. The world is always showing off in microscopic ways; most of us are busy performing the role of Human Who Has Seen Everything.

Evening came in layers: amber on brick, violet on glass, a sodium lamp waking like a cautious moon. Somewhere a violin practiced the same four notes with devotion and errors. The city made its imperfect chords—engine, bird, radiator, laugh, distant train. If harmony means no friction, we will never have it. If harmony means friction held in tension, then this is music of a very local kind.

I won’t pretend every day is a revelation. Some days are administrative. Some days are oatmeal without ceremony. Some days the silence is not wisdom but only a room refusing to be interesting. Still, even the blank ones are proof that we were somewhere, awake, passing through the narrow corridor between yesterday and tomorrow with our portable astonishment.

The unfinished map remains unfinished because an accurate one would be the death of wandering. Let there be unknowns in the margins: a city we haven’t forgiven, an island of courage, the blue uncharted province where we stop apologizing for not being finished products. Maybe completion is a rumor started by people allergic to surprise. Maybe we are not meant to arrive but to widen.

So here is the offering, roughly a thousand words of looking: a kettle, a cloud like a trout, tomatoes planted against advice, a parking-meter gentleman, violin notes stumbling toward beauty, and the stubborn human habit of noticing before the light goes. Not a masterpiece—more a bowl of warm rice for the inner animal. Eat slowly. There is enough to go around, despite appearances.

Outside, night settles its dark coat over roofs and antennas. The bus sighs again. The herbs sleep on their balcony. Somewhere a galaxy keeps refining its ridiculous glitter. I close the notebook with ink still wet and a map still wrong, grateful for the errors, grateful for the margin, grateful that something in me still believes a person is not a final draft but a doorway, leaning, as all doorways must, toward the light.
